newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Australia opposed to human rights clause in EU deal.
newsitem.headline: Australia opposed to human rights clause in EU deal.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said Canberra remained firmly opposed to an agreement with the European Union that included a human rights clause.
Speaking to an Australian business group meeting on Wednesday, Downer said the clause -- included as a matter of course in all bilateral agreements the EU signs -- was one-sided and subjective.

"We are a gutsy, up-front country and making something of this," he said. "There is, however, a great deal of interest from other governments as to how Australia handles the issue. It is something that transcends Australia."
Downer, in Brussels for talks on a so-called Framework Agreement which details Australian-EU relations, said there was no question that Canberra did not support human rights.

"We have a very proud record ... not a country in the world can match our record on human rights," he said. "But what kind of a deal allows one party to terminate it on the basis of one-sided, subjective observation.
"The framework agreement is purely symbolic. It contains no trade concessions and no access conditions so it seems this clause is unneccessary."
The clause, included as a matter of course in all EU agreements with other countries, allows the 15-nation bloc to break off relations in the event of human rights abuses in that country.

Downer will meet European Commission officials later on Monday for talks on the issue and diplomatic sources say the deal may be scrapped and replaced by a more bland "statement of mutual recognition".
Downer told the Australian Business in Europe forum that while Asia would remain the main focus for Australian trade, the EU remained a vital market.

"First and foremost our own region is what we are focused on," he said. "But relations with Europe are very important to us ... although we cannot be happy until we have an equitable agriculture policy."
Downer blamed European restrictions on Australia's agriculture and energy sectors for a trade deficit with the EU but said Canberra would continue to press for their removal.
He said Australia had a vibrant, growing economy "that by all standards would be among the forerunners for meeting the convergence criteria required by EMU (economic and monetary union)".
